categories.label: Time signals
categories.reason: on all day, every day; the first thing to try on a new radio

categories.label: Beacons
categories.reason: tell you which bands are open, and to where

categories.label: Weather

categories.label: Calling frequencies
categories.reason: where people listen for a call

landmarks.name: WWV / WWVH
landmarks.line: The loudest of the set in daylight
landmarks.hear: A tick every second, a tone most minutes, and a voice giving the UTC time just before each minute. A man's voice is WWV in Colorado; a woman's voice is WWVH in Hawaii.
landmarks.why: It runs all day from two sites on several frequencies, so it is the standard check that a radio hears anything at all. One of them is almost always readable somewhere in North America.
landmarks.try: Compare the announced time with the clock at the top of POTACAT. If they are more than a second apart, FT8 will decode poorly; Station Setup checks the clock.

landmarks.line: The night-time frequency, best after dark

landmarks.name: WWV / WWVH
landmarks.line: Good at night and in the early morning

landmarks.name: WWV / WWVH
landmarks.line: Daytime, longer distances

landmarks.name: WWV
landmarks.line: Daytime only, and only when the high bands are open

landmarks.name: CHU
landmarks.line: Canada's time signal, strong in the east at night
landmarks.hear: A tick every second, a voice announcing the time in English and French each minute, and a short burst of data tones between seconds 31 and 39.
landmarks.why: Canada's official time signal, on three frequencies. 7850 sits just above the 40 m band and is strong across eastern North America after dark.
landmarks.try: On a quiet evening, tune 7850 and then 3330. Which one is louder tells you how far the signal is travelling tonight.

landmarks.line: Canada's time signal, the night-time frequency

landmarks.name: CHU
landmarks.line: Canada's time signal, the daytime frequency

landmarks.name: RWM
landmarks.line: Russia's time signal. A real DX catch
landmarks.hear: Short carrier pulses, one per second, with a longer pulse at each minute, and a Morse ident now and then. No voice.
landmarks.why: Russia's time signal from near Moscow. Hearing it in North America means the path across the Atlantic and Europe is open on that band.
landmarks.try: Use a narrow CW filter and listen for the once-a-second pulses under the noise. Then try 4996 after dark.

landmarks.name: RWM
landmarks.line: Russia's time signal, the night-time frequency

landmarks.name: WWVB
landmarks.line: The signal that sets radio-controlled clocks
landmarks.hear: No voice and no ticks you would recognise. The carrier drops in strength at the start of every second, which sounds like a slow, steady beat in CW mode.
landmarks.why: It sets the radio-controlled clocks and watches across North America from Fort Collins, Colorado. Hearing it on a ham radio shows how far down your receiver really goes.
landmarks.try: It is easiest at night with a long wire antenna. Watch the S-meter dip once a second rather than listening for a tone.

landmarks.name: DCF77
landmarks.line: Germany's clock signal. Very hard from the Americas
landmarks.hear: A carrier that drops in strength at the start of each second, like WWVB. No voice.
landmarks.why: It sets the radio-controlled clocks of Europe. From North America it takes a quiet winter night and a large antenna, which makes it a prize.
landmarks.try: Listen on a European KiwiSDR from the SDR menu first, so you know what you are looking for.

landmarks.name: NCDXF / IARU beacons
landmarks.line: 18 beacons around the world take turns
landmarks.hear: A callsign in Morse, then four one-second dashes, each ten times weaker than the one before: 100 W, 10 W, 1 W and a tenth of a watt.
landmarks.why: Eighteen beacons on five continents share this frequency, ten seconds each, every three minutes. Each dash you hear is a path that is open right now, and the weakest dash you can hear shows how much margin it has.
landmarks.try: Stay for three minutes and note which beacons come through. Then try 28200: if any beacon is there, 10 m is open and worth a CQ.

landmarks.name: NCDXF / IARU beacons
landmarks.line: The same beacons on 17 m, one turn later

landmarks.name: NOAA Weather Radio WX1
landmarks.line: Forecasts and warnings, read around the clock
landmarks.hear: A computer voice reading the forecast, current conditions and any warnings for the area around the transmitter, on a loop.
landmarks.why: More than a thousand transmitters cover the US on seven channels. In a storm it is the fastest way to hear warnings, and it is a handy check of a 2 m antenna.
landmarks.try: Click through the seven channels. The strongest one is your local transmitter; a weaker one is usually the next county over.

landmarks.name: Shannon VOLMET
landmarks.line: Airport weather for aircraft over the Atlantic
landmarks.hear: A recorded voice reading the weather at European airports in a fixed order: wind, visibility, cloud, temperature and pressure.
landmarks.why: It runs around the clock from Ireland for aircraft crossing the Atlantic. Clear copy in North America means the path to Europe is open.
landmarks.try: The lower frequencies work at night and the higher ones by day. Try all four and note which one is readable now.

landmarks.name: 2 m national simplex
landmarks.line: Call here, then move to another frequency
landmarks.hear: Silence most of the time, then someone calling a callsign or saying they are monitoring.
landmarks.why: It is the national FM simplex calling frequency in the US. Every 2 m radio can reach it, so it is where a traveller or a new ham calls first.
landmarks.try: Leave it on while you work. When someone calls, answer, then agree on another frequency and move off.

landmarks.line: The 70 cm FM calling frequency

landmarks.name: 1.25 m national simplex
landmarks.line: The 1.25 m FM calling frequency

landmarks.name: 6 m FM simplex
landmarks.line: The 6 m FM calling frequency

landmarks.name: 2 m SSB calling
landmarks.line: Where weak-signal VHF stations meet
landmarks.hear: Mostly quiet. During contests and band openings, SSB and CW stations calling CQ, often from a few hundred miles away.
landmarks.why: The 2 m SSB calling frequency. Weak-signal work on VHF uses sideband and horizontal antennas, and stations meet here before moving up the band.
landmarks.try: During a VHF contest or on a Sunday morning, point a horizontal antenna toward the nearest city and listen here.

landmarks.name: 70 cm SSB calling
landmarks.line: Where weak-signal UHF stations meet

landmarks.name: 6 m SSB calling
landmarks.line: Check here when 6 m opens in summer
landmarks.hear: Usually nothing. When the band opens, stations from hundreds of miles away, sometimes for only a few minutes.
landmarks.why: The 6 m SSB calling frequency. Summer sporadic-E openings show up here first.
landmarks.try: From May to August, check here around midday and early evening. If you hear anyone at all, the band is open.

landmarks.name: 20 m QRP CW
landmarks.line: Low-power CW, often from a park or a summit
landmarks.hear: Morse from stations running a few watts, many of them portable.
landmarks.why: The QRP CW calling frequency on 20 m. Activators running a small radio from a park or a hilltop often sit near it.
landmarks.try: Listen around 14060 on a weekend afternoon. The weak signal you can barely copy may be five watts and a wire in a tree.

landmarks.name: 40 m QRP CW
landmarks.line: Low-power CW on 40 m

landmarks.name: 20 m QRP SSB
landmarks.line: Low-power voice contacts
landmarks.hear: Voice stations running low power, calling CQ QRP.
landmarks.why: The QRP SSB calling frequency on 20 m. Low-power stations meet here so they are not lost among the big signals.
landmarks.try: If you run a portable radio, call here and say you are QRP. Stations listening will expect a weak signal.

landmarks.name: Marine channel 16
landmarks.line: Distress and calling on the water. Listen only
landmarks.hear: Coast Guard broadcasts and boats hailing each other before moving to a working channel.
landmarks.why: Channel 16 is the distress and calling channel for boats. Hams may listen, but may not transmit there.
landmarks.try: Near a coast or the Great Lakes, listen for a Coast Guard broadcast; it names the channel it is about to move to.

landmarks.name: Aviation emergency
landmarks.line: The aircraft guard frequency. Listen only
landmarks.hear: Usually silence. Now and then a pilot asked to check in, or the sweeping tone of an emergency beacon.
landmarks.why: 121.5 MHz is the aviation emergency frequency, monitored by air traffic control and many aircraft. Hams may listen, but may not transmit there.

landmarks.name: CB channel 19
landmarks.line: Truck drivers on the highway. Listen only
landmarks.hear: Truck drivers talking about traffic, weather and the road ahead.
landmarks.why: The busiest CB channel on US highways. A ham radio may receive it, but may not transmit there.
landmarks.try: Near an interstate, tune it for a live traffic report.

landmarks.name: CB channel 9
landmarks.line: The CB emergency channel. Listen only

landmarks.name: The Buzzer (UVB-76)
landmarks.line: A Russian buzz every two seconds since the 1970s
landmarks.hear: A short buzz, about 25 a minute, day and night. A few times a month a voice reads out words and numbers.
landmarks.why: Nobody outside Russia knows what it is for. It is the most listened-to mystery on shortwave, and hearing it from the Americas takes a good antenna and a good night.
landmarks.try: Try after dark with the noise blanker off. If it is too weak here, open a European KiwiSDR from the SDR menu and hear what you are missing.

landmarks.name: SAQ Grimeton
landmarks.line: A 1924 alternator transmitter, on the air a few times a year
landmarks.hear: Slow, hand-sent Morse from the only working alternator transmitter left in the world.
landmarks.why: Grimeton in Sweden is a UNESCO World Heritage site. It goes on the air a few times a year, including Alexanderson Day in summer and Christmas Eve.
landmarks.try: Most HF radios cannot tune 17.2 kHz. On the day, listen through a European KiwiSDR, and send a reception report for a QSL card.
